title: My Nephew Sold My Shares While I Was at the Cardiologist—But He Made One Terrible Mistake

blocks.text: My nephew Travis sold my shares in Hollis Feed and Seed while I was 47 miles away at a cardiology appointment.
He told the buyer I was “old enough to be confused.”
Then he texted me three words that still make my blood run cold:
He thought he was taking advantage of an old woman.
What he didn’t know was that I had spent my entire life learning exactly what people do when they think you’re too old to fight back.
I had owned 38 percent of Hollis Feed and Seed since my brother Paul died.
Paul and I had built that store together long before Travis was old enough to spell “feed.”
When soy prices crashed one year, I paid the loan.
When Paul’s widow needed surgery, I worked the counter for six straight weeks.
I knew which farmers would argue over fifty cents and which ones would quietly leave a hundred-dollar tip in December.
I could even tell by the smell when a bag of feed had gotten damp in the back room.
Once, I even gave his mother money for groceries when I knew perfectly well she was going to use most of it to cover rent.
Then Travis came back from Tulsa wearing shiny shoes and using words like “modernize,” “restructure,” and “maximize the asset.”
He started replacing longtime employees.
He complained about customers who still paid by check.
He wanted to turn the old feed store into something “sleek.”
I told him farmers didn’t care if the walls were sleek.
They cared if you had their feed when they needed it.
“That’s why we need younger leadership, Aunt Jean.”
I should have listened to the warning in his voice.
The cardiology appointment was in Springfield.
My daughter Ellen drove me because she says I follow trucks too closely.
After the appointment, we stopped at Dollar General for paper towels and peppermint candy.
I turned my phone back on in the parking lot.
Thank you for making the transition smooth.
I hope you’re comfortable with the new arrangement.
Aunt Jean, this is mercy. You need to let the next generation take over.
You’re old enough to be confused about the paperwork anyway.
At home, I walked directly to my bedroom.
Behind an old quilt box was a small steel safe.
Inside were tax records, old photographs, Paul’s handwritten notes—and the original buy-sell agreement for Hollis Feed and Seed.
The agreement was signed nine years earlier.
And there, in black ink, was the clause Travis had apparently forgotten.
No ownership interest could be transferred without written consent from the other shareholders.
Colton was the largest customer Hollis Feed and Seed had.
He bought more feed in a month than some customers bought in a year.
And Travis desperately needed his business.
“Colton,” I said, “how much did Travis charge you for my shares?”
Travis was standing behind the counter wearing a new jacket.
I put the buy-sell agreement on the counter.
He had attempted to sell something that didn’t belong to him.
Except Paul’s estate had already been settled.
And the shares had been redistributed years earlier.
“Jean, did Paul leave anything besides the store?”
I told her about an old locked cabinet in Paul’s office.
It was dated three weeks before his death.
“Jean, if Travis ever tries to take control of the store, don’t fight him over the business.”
He had written that Travis had been secretly taking money from the store.
He had also discovered that Travis had been falsifying supplier invoices.
At the bottom of the letter, Paul wrote:
“I don’t want my son to inherit control of what we built. If he ever attempts to sell my shares without permission, use the attached agreement.”
And it contained something I had never known.
Paul had transferred his remaining interest into a protected family trust.
The next morning, I returned to Hollis Feed and Seed with my attorney.
“Travis,” I said, “you didn’t sell my shares.”
“You sold something that wasn’t yours to sell.”
But then my attorney opened one final document.
The $186,000 he’d received from Colton hadn’t gone toward buying the business.
